Indian IT Professionals in Germany 
*182. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large number of IT professionals arc in demand 
in Germany; 
(b) if so. how many Indians had gone there during last one year; and 
(c) what efforts arc being made to increase the quota of Indians being sent 
there? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (SHRI PRAMOD 
MAHAJAN): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. Since 1st August 2000, Germany has been issuing 
special work permits to skilled IT professionals from Non-EU (European Union) 
Countries, including India. As of 16th February 2001, a total of 1046 special 
work permits have been issued to 
Indians. 
2 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Sir, the Federal Chancellor of Germany, 
Mr. Gerhard Schroder in the month of August, 2000, gave grccn signal to the "Green 
Card" Scheme, initially, inviting 20,000 IT professionals from India. It was only 
an initial ceiling; and the Government of Germany is thinking of increasing the 
quota to more than 30,000 jobs a year. According to my information, in 2000 itself, 
about 50,000 IT professionals were employed from within and outside Germany in 
this sector. I would like to know how the Government is pursuing the getting of 
"Grccn Cards" exclusively to the Indian IT professionals and how is it that we 
could send only 1,000 odd IT professionals to Germany last year when we 
have so many professionals? 
The other important point is, there is no doubt that there are avenues in 
Germany, particularly, in networking and next generation c-infrastructurc solutions 
but there arc limited growth opportunities for our IT people, education in an alien 
language for their children, and a bove all fears of racism and rightwing 
violence. How the Government is going to address all these problems? 
Part (b) of my supplementary is, what efforts the Ministry is making, with 
the help of our Foreign Ministry and Germany, with regard to having a modern 
migration policy for protection of our IT professionals in Germany. 
SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Sir, the green card system provides about 
10,000 grccn cards to non-European citizens of the world to work in Germany 
for the next 3 years. Under this green card system, the validity of the work permit 
is for 5 years, and the quota decided by Germany for non-European countries is 
about 10,000, for the next three years. It may be increased—if they need—to 
20,000. As recently as on 16th February, 2001, Germany had issued green cards 
to 5,403 persons of non-European Union nations. Out of this, 1,046 grccn cards 
have been issued to Indians. Basically, these Indians are cither directly employed 
persons or persons employed through different companies. The Government of 
India does not send persons to Germany. There is no such scheme of sending 
people to Germany. Bui out of 5,000 grccn card holders, roughly 1,000 are 
Indians. One

DR. RAJA RAM ANNA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, we arc very proud that 
Indians are greatly in demand in this highly specialised subject, even by the 
very advanced countries. But we have to take note of the fact that we should 
not send a large number of our best men for this subject alone, because the 
country has begun to suffer in other fields. In oiden days, this country was

work in different countries, naturally, they are likely to f ace some kind of 
problems of work permits, taxation, double taxation, social security taxation, 
visa restrictions etc. These problems will naturally arise. Government is naturally 
keeping a vigil on these issues. Whenever such issues come up, the External 
Affairs

Ministry competently deals with them . If any such complaint comes to my 
Ministry, with the co-operation of the External Affairs Ministry, we will deal 
with it. I do not see any major complaint at this juncture for the very simple 
reason that Indians are more than welcome in those countries. I can say that the IT 
industry in many countries is eating out of the hands of Indians. So, at this 
juncture, these are not the problems, but we will definitely keep a strict watch on

urban areas and among English speaking people. So, the real challenge before India

West to East, from cities to villages and from English-speaking people to Indian 
language speaking people. That is what is called as 'IT for the masses'. We

report. We are taking many initiatives to take IT to the masses.

1315. SHRI VEDPRAKASH P. GOYAL: Will the Minister of

 what steps are being taken by Government during the last two years, to 
increase the level of global cooperation in the field of agriculture;

56 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) to (d) India has taken effective steps 
to increase the level of global cooper ation in the field of agriculture. 
Agreements/Memorandum of Understandings (MoUs) have been signed with 
39 countries for bilateral cooperation in the field of agriculture, including 
phytosanitary and veterinary agreements. Out of these 39 countries, 
Agrecments/MoUs with IS countries were  signed during the last two years. 
The objective of bilateral Agreements/M oUs is to exchange experiences of 
agricultural development between countries and to extend mutual benefit and 
cooperation for each other's development. 
The Agreements on plant quarantine and plant protection and in the 
veterinary field aim, inter*alia, at the prevention of the penetration and 
spreading of quarantine pests, plant diseases and weeds and spread of 
infective diseases on the territories of both the countries while trading in 
agricultural products, animal products, raw materials of animal origin and 
animal feed. These kind of agreements facilitate development India's trade in 
agricultural and veterinary products with these countries. 
India is an active member of several international organizations, such as 
United Nations Food & Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and World Food 
Programme. India is also a beneficiar y of the programmes of all these 
organisations. 
India continues to have active inter-action with other countries through 
exhange visits of scientists, training programmes etc. to share each others' 
experiences in the field of agricultural research and education and 
agricultural development.

RESOLUTION 
In order to reduce storage and transit losses of foodgrains at farm an 
commercial level, to modernise the system of handling, storage and 
transportation of the foodgrains procured by the Food Corporation of India 
(FCI) and to bring in additionality of resources through private sector involvement, 
the Government has approved a National Policy on Handling, Storage and 
Transportation of Foodgrains, details of which are given below:— 
1. Objectives of the Policy 
The main objectives of the policy are: 
(i) to reduce storage and trasnsit losses at farm level where about 70% 
of the total foodgrain production is retained and consumed and also to 
encourage the farmers to adopt scientific storage methods. 
(ii) to modernise the system of handling storage and transportation of the 
foodgrains procured by the Food Corporation of India (FCI). 
(iii) to harness efforts and resources of public and private sectors, both 
domestic and foreign, to build and operate infrastructure for introduction 
of bulk handling, storage and transportation of foodgrains in the 
country. 
2. Policy for house-hold storage 
2.1 Since the house-hold sector retains about 70% of the total production and 
substantial quantities of foodgrains are wasted due to improper storage at 
farm level, the major focus is on the improvement of storage standards at 
farm level. Presently, the only scheme targeting this need is the Save 
Grain Campaign, which popularises the use of metallic and non-metallic 
storage structures and educates the farmers about the adoption of scientific 
storage methods. The scheme also aims at developmentfmprovement of 
non-metalic traditional storage structures. 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
2.2 In order to have a greater success in this area, following initiatives 
have been approved:— 
(i) intrpduction of a scheme to encour age use of metal bins as well as 
non-metallic storage structures at individual farm level and 
construction of RCC bins at community level with appropriate 
financial incentives. 
(ii) strengthening of the existing research and training components of the 
Save Grain Campaign Scheme for scientific storage and preservation 
of foodgrains and their propagation among farmers. 
3.    Modernisation    and    Upgradation    of   Bulk    Grain    Handling 
Infrastructure 
3.1 In order to reduce storage losses, it is necessary to develop and 
modernise the infrastructure for integrated bulk handling, 
storage and transportation in India. The thrust of the policy 
should be:— 
(i) encouragement   of   mechanical   harvesting,   cleaning   and 
drying at farm and mandi level. 
(ii) transportation of gr ains from farm to silos by specially designed 
trucks. 
(iii) construction of a chain of silos at procurement as well as distribution 
points. 
(iv) transportation of grain from silos to railhead and thereafter to pre-
determined destinations by specially designed trucks' rail wagons 
(with top filling and bottom discharge mechanismydedicated trains. 
(v) declaration of foodgrains storage as infrastructure. 
3.2 For storage of foodgrains procured by the FCI, integrated bulk 
handling facilities with silos of large capacity for wheat along 
with testing facilities for quality control would be created at 
about 20 identified central locations in producing and 
consuming areas as well as a few port towns. These facilities, 
including the infrastructure for bulk transportation to these 
92 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
centres, will be created and maintained in the private sector under the 
overall co-ordination of the FCI. The design of special top filling and 
bottom discharge wagons would be decided in consultation with the 
Ministry of Railways. The Ministry of Railways will also be consulted 
while deciding the locations and the circuits where these wagons would 
ply. FCI will guarantee utilisation of these facilities to the extent of 
100% for the first ten years and 75% for the next ten years. From these 
points, secondary transportation of foodgrains would be made in bag 
form to about 500 godowns in important central locations in different 
States to be owned and maintained by the FCI. Further transportation to 
the consuming centres for retail distribution under the Public Distribution 
System will be carried out by the State Governments. 
 The private sector will be encouraged to build storage capac ities in 
which they will store and maintain foodgrains procured by the Government 
agencies, for which they will be entitled to storage charges. 
 The private sector participation should be sought and encouraged   for   
development   of   infrastructure   for   the 
integrated     bulk     handling,    storage    and    transportation through— 
(i) measures such as Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT), Build-Own-
Lease-Transfer (BOLT), Build-Own-Operate (BOO), Lease-Develop-
Operate (LDO), Joint Ventures etc. 
(ii) generation   of   funds   through   public   issues   by   private 
enterprises. 
(iii) automatic approval for Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) upto 100%. 
(iv) loans   from   financial   institutions,   NABARD,   external 
commercial borrowings. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
(v) fiscal incentives as given below: 
 100% deduction in profit for the purpose of Income Tax for 
the first five years and 30% deduction in profit for the next five 
years. 
 deduction of 40% of the profits derived by financial 
institutions financing such projects, as provided to financial 
corporations engaged, inter-alia, in providing long term finance 
for agricultural development. 
 customs duty exemption for items not manufactured in 
India, on a case-to-case basis, su bject to a list of such equipment 
being submitted in advance. 
4. Development of Infrastructure Facilities at Ports 
India has been traditionally the importer of foodgrains and, therefore, the 
infrastructure facilities available at the ports are basically meant of unloading 
operations and not for exports. For unloading operations, ship gears are 
normally used. Even the latest mechanised facilities at Jawaharlal Nehru 
Port, Navi Mumbai have been designed for import purposes only. There is 
also lack of general cargo berths at the major ports and very limited 
warehousing facihties are available for the storage of foodgrains at ports. For 
creating the proper port facilities for foodgrains meant for export in due 
course, the infrastructure facilities wo uld have to be developed for which 
following actions are required: 
(i) identification of ports to be developed for purposes of export of 
foodgrains. The distribution of foodgrains traffic may spread over to the non-
traditional ports which have spare capacity like New Mangalore and Cochin 
ports; 
(ii) development of more general cargo berths at the ports through ports* 
own investmentfcrivate participation; 
(iii) water front-berths can be leased to the users who may be encouraged 
to put up their own facilities; and 
(iv) development of dedicated modern foodgrains handling facilities at 
selected ports. 
94 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
5. Role of the Central Government 
The Central Government would: 
 facilitate speedy clearance of projects concerning development of 
infrastructure for bulk handling, transportation and storage of foodgrains by setting 
up an Approval Board competent to take final decision; 
 enter into bilateral agreements with other countries 7 international 
agencies for providing technicakfinancial assistance; 
 take necessary legislative/administrative measures for removing 
impediments with regard to stock control Orderymovement control Orders 
framed by various State Governments; 
 utilize the services of an existing independent regulatory mechanism for 
fixingfegulating tariff for various operations, such as cleaning, drying, storage, 
transportation, etc.; 
 make    available    facilities    of    the    Railways    for    bulk 
transportation; 
 promote negotiable Warehouse Recei pt System by which farmers 
could hold their grains back from market and meet their working capital&hort 
term requirement by borrowing from Banks against these receipts; and 
 promote research for development of alternate storage technologies 
like Vacuum Process Storage (VPS) technology which 
would ensure longer shelf life of foodgrains and help export of foodgrains in 
vacuum packs. 
6. Role of the State Government 
The State Government would help in: 
 acquisition of land required for various projects as for public purpose; and 
 making available other facilities such as water, power, road, etc.

Population below Poverty Line 
1353. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: W ill the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the number of people living below Poverty Line 
varied according to the assessment made by the States/ Planning Commission; 
105

 if so, the details thereof indicating the methods used by the 
States/Planning Commission to count BPL population; 
 the details of the fund allotted during the years 1999, 2000 and 2001 
per head for the upliftment of BPL population; and 
 the number of BPL population benefited under PDS and the number of 
BPL population as on date, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM 
CHAUHAN): (a) and (b) There are va rious estimates of the number of 
people living below poverty line (BPL). 
State Governments identify the families living below poverty line at the 
behest of Ministry of Rural Development on the basis of BPL census 
conducted at the beginning of the Five Year Plan. The BPL Census as per the 
BPL schedules is conducted in two phases. The 
first phase covers all the rural households and the data on assets and income 
is collected for the purpose of exclusion of non BPL families. 
In the second phase a BPL household is defined on the basis of the monthly 
per capita expenditure. If the per capita household expenditure is less than 
the poverty line the household is defined as poor. 
The Planning Commission estimates the percentage of persons living 
below the poverty line at national and state level from the large sample 
surveys on consumer expenditure conducted by the National Sample Survey 
Organisation (NSSO). The poverty line is defined in terms of expenditure per 
person per month. Based on the recommendations of the Expert Group on 
Estimation of Proportion and Number of Poor (Lakdawala Committes) the 
Government has applied state-specific poverty estimates in order to identify 
the poor i.e., persons living below the poverty line (BPL). These State-wise 
106 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
poverty estimates have been worked out by the Planning Commission from the 
national level poverty lines, using state- specific price indices and inter-state 
price differentials. The national poverty lines are expressed as monthly per 
capita consumption expenditure of Rs. 49.09 in rural areas and Rs. 56.64 in 
urban areas at 1973-74 prices corresponding to a basket of goods and services 
anchored on a norm of per capita daily calorie requirement of 2400 kcal in 
rural areas and 2100 kcal in urban areas . These percentage are applied to the 
estimated population in order to arrive at the number of persons living below 
the poverty line. 
The percentage of poor families in BPL census conducted by the States is 
suspected to have an upward bias in estimation of poor families because the 
survey is conducted with the specific purpose of identifying families for self 
selection as beneficiaries in various poverty alleviation programme. 
Allocation of foodgrains under TPDS for BPL families is made on the 
combined BPL population (for rural and urban) estimated by Planning 
Commission and not only for rural BPL population identified by States under 
BPL census. 
(c) Funds allotted to States under various schemes of Ministry of

population during 1999-2000 and 2000-2001 are as per Statement-I 
(See below). Funds allocated by the Ministry of Rural Development

Planning Commission.

Dumping of Sugar 
1357. SHRI JIBON ROY: Will the Mi nister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that dumping of sugar and failure to meet the 
export target have together created an unmarketable stock of 100 lakh 
tonnes; and 
 if so, what steps have been taken by Government to save the industry 
and the sugarcane growers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. 
SREENIVASA PRASAD): (a) No, Sir. However due to record sugar 
production of 181.4 lakh tonnes in the 1999-2000 sugar season, the carried 
forward stock as 1.10.2000 was high, provisionally estimated at 92.97 lakh 
tonnes. 
(b) In order to improve the financial health of the sugar industry and their 
capacity to pay the cane price to sugarc ane growers as also to liquidate the 
cane price arrears, the Government has taken the following steps: 
(i) Levy Obligation on sugar mills has been reduced from 40% to 30%  
w.e.f.  1.1.2000 and again to 15% w.e.f. 1.2.2001. 
(ii) Custom duty on imported sugar has been increased to 60% w.e.f 
9.2.2000 along with continuance of the countervailing 
duty of Rs. 850 per tonne so as to restrict inflow of sugar into the 
country. 
(iii) Pursuing a  policy of encouraging stability anej  reasonable 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
level of sugar prices in the domestic market through judicious releases 
of freesale sugar quotas. 
(iv) Advanced releases of freesale sugar.to needy sugar mills are being 
given to enable them to clear can price dues of the 
farmers. 
(v) Export of 10 lakh tonnes'of sugar has been permitted. In order to boost 
export of sugar, Government has taken the following measures; 
 The sugar meant for export has been exempted from levy 
obligation. This exemption, which was initially available for a period 
of six months, commencing from 1st June 2000, has been extended 
upto 31st March 2001. 
 It has been decided to treat the quantity exported for commercial  
exports  as  advance  free  sale  release  to  be 
adjusted after a period of 12 months from the date of release. 
 It has also been decided that the levy exemption on the quantity of 
sugar meant for commercial exports, if it cannot be availed by the 
sugar factory out of 1999-2000 season's production due to the 
completion of its levy obligation, may be availed by the concerned 
sugar factory from the production in the ensuing sugar season. 
 DEPB at the rate of 5% of the F.O.B. value of exports of sugar has 
been allowed. 
Increase in Food Stock 
1358. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA': Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIR, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
 whether Government faced difficulties due to massive increase in food 
stock in Central pool this year; 
 if so, the reasons therefor; 
116 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
 what are its ramifications; and 
 the measures being taken for tackling this problem? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM 
CHAUHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Due to record procurement of  both wheat and rice, and lower 
off take under various welfare schemes including the Public 
Distribution System (PDS), the stocks of Foodgrains have 
accumulated in the Central Pool. 
(c) and (d) The carrying cost of buffer stocks has increased. 
However, the following steps have been taken to liquidate the surplus 
stocks over and above the buffer norms; 
(i) Open Sale of wheat at reduced prices has been started from 
11.07.2000; 
(ii) Open sale of rice has been started from 04.09.2000; 
(iii) The Central Issue Prices of wheat and rice were revised downwards 
from 25.7.2000; 
(iv) The CIPs of wheat and rice for APL farmilies have been fixed at 100% 
of the Economic cost or the open Market Sale prices decided by the 
FCI from time to time, whichever is lower. The Open Market rates 
being less than the economic cost, the States can avail of this offer 
and make foodgrains available to  APL population at these reduced 
rates; 
(v) The allocation of foodgrains for Below Poverty Line (BPL) families @ 
20 kg. per family per months is now being made on the basis of 
Population Projections of the Registrar General as on 01.03.2000 
instead of projected population of 1995; 
(vi) Foodgrains at BPL rates are available for allotment to State 
Governments @5 kg. per head per month for covering categories of 
indigent people living in welfare institutions such as beggar homes, 
hostels for SC/ST/backward students/Nari Niketans etc. sponsored by 
the State Governments and the con cerned administrative Ministry of 
the Government of India. 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
Foodgrains can now be allocated under the Annapoorna scheme to 
indigent old persons even in th e case of those receiving old age 
pension from the State Governments; 
(vii) Foodgrains at CIP applicable for BPL families is being allocated for 
all welfare schemes implemented by the various Ministries of the 
Government of India; 
(viii) Foodgrains at the rates applicable for BPL families are being allotted 
to the State Governments for undertaking "Food for Work" 
programmes in the States, as also for the Greening India Campaign; 
(ix) Foodgrains are being allocated at BPL rates for development schemes 
(where the beneficiaries belong to the BPL category), implemented by 
NGOs sponsored by the State Go vernments and endorsed by the 
administrative Ministry in the Government of India as also by the 
International Organisations like the World Food Programme; 
(x) FCI has been permitted to offer wheat for export at a price not lower 
than the CIP for BPL category, which, at present is Rs. 4150 7- per 
MT.; 
(xi) Government have also launched Antodya Anna Yojna on 5.12.2000 
and under this scheme Government plans to release wheat and rice @ 
Rs. 2/- and Rs. 3/- per kg. respectively subject to 25 kg. per family 
per month to approximate on crore poorest families all over the 
country and the State Governments have accordingly been requested 
to identify these families; 
(xii) The State Warehousing Corporations in the procuring States are 
creating Storage capacity for the us e of FCI to meet the increased 
procurement; 
(xiii) Government. has also formulated a National Storage Policy aimed at 
harnessing the resources of public and Private Sector for 
augmentation of infrastructure to handle foodgrains including 
construction of bulk and conventional storage facilities at the 
strategic Centres.

G.A.G. Report on PDS 
1360.   SHRI   PREM   CHAND   GUPTA:   Will   the   Minister  of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD  AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased 
to state: 
 whether it is a fact that the recent  report of the CAG for the year 
ending March, 1999 points out that the PDS continues to be plagued be 
problems such as ineffective implementation, poor administration; 
 whether it is also a fact that alt hough the subsidy increased from Rs. 
2,800 crore in 1992 to Rs. 8,700 crore in 1997, the weaker section did not 
benefit much from this; and 
 if so, what are Government's views on this report and action taken 
thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM 
CHAUHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) The report of the CAG covers the period 1992-1999. Targeted 
Public Distribution System was launched in June, 1997 with its focus on the 
poor ensuring 10 kg. of foodgrains per family per month at highly subsidised 
prices. Keeping in view the need to in crease the allocation of foodgrains for 
the BPL families and to better targetisc the food subsidy, Government Of 
India has increased the allocation to BPL families from 10 kg. to 20 kg. of 
foodgrains per family per month at 50% of economic cost from April 1, 2000. 
The Central Issue Prices for APL have been fixed at 100% of economic cost 
from the same date. The entire consumer subsidy has been directed for the 
benefit of BPL population with the above changes. 
Public Distribution System is implemented under the joint responsibility of 
the Central and State Government/ UT Administration. The Central 
Government is responsible for procurement, storage and transportation of the 
PDS commodities up to the designated central godowns and making them 
available to the 
120 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
States. The responsibility for distribution to the consumers through the fair 
price shops and administrations of the PDS rests with the State Government. 
Extracts of the CAG's report arc bein g forwarded to the State Government 
and UT Administration for taking appropriate steps for removing the 
deficiencies in implementation of PDS. 
The State Governments have been requested to closely monitor the PDS at 
the Fair Price Shops (FPS) and other levels and to make arrangement for 
distribution of PDS commodities in a transparent and accountable manner by 
involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs). Involvement of 
Panchayati Raj Institutions in the implementation of TPDS as a measure of 
social audit will make the system more transparent and accountable.

1408. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of LABOUR 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to generate employment 
opportunities  on   large-scale   for   removing  unemployment   in   the

productive employment which will be generated* in the growth process itself

implemented as a central Plan scheme to provide employment opportunities

Upgrading Skills of Work Force 
1410. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Will the Minister of 
LABOUR be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that globalisation has thrown open our industrial and 
other economic sectors to face stiff competition from foreign products; 
 if so, whether it is also a fact that in order to be more competitive it is 
essential to work out a joint strategy between Government employees and 
trade unions to upgrade skills of the 
workforce; and 
(c) if so, what measures are being taken to achieve this objective? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL): (a) to (c) It is a fact that globalisation requires the industrial sector 
to improve its competitiveness in the world economy through upgradation of 
skills of the workforce. In the Budget for 2001-2002, it has been recognised 
that the economy's competitiveness can be strengthened through human 
resource development. A Task Force has been set up under the Human 
Resource Development Minister which has been making wide ranging 
recommendations to upgrade and expand technology education. The base of IITs 
is being expanded, engineering colleges are being strengthened and new 
institutes are to be set up with public-private partnership. A new centrally sponsored

initiatives are to be taken for encouraging IT education from school to college

Labour Market Reforms 
1411. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that only little headway has been made in bringing 
about labour market reforms in the country; and 
 if so, what steps Government have taken so far to convince the trade 
unions and workers that a flexible labour market alone would mean "more" 
and not fewer jobs in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL): (a) and (b) Labour being one of the important factors of 
production, its role has vital implications for production and productive processes 
and consequently for the status of the economy. A large number of labour 
laws have been framed over a period of time to address a number of issues 
and problems that assumed importance and attracted pointed attention at a 
particular point of time. The process of liberalization, economic reforms and 
structural adjustment was set in motion in 1991. This was followed by changes in 
the fiscal regime, trade policy, foreign and investment policy and restructuring 
of Public Sector. The main objective of all these changes was to make the Indian 
industry more competitive. As most of the labour legislations were enacted long 
time back these require certian changes. In order to ensure both consistency of 
labour laws with the general changes taking place in the economic policy and to 
provide for health, safety and welfare of the working class, the Second National 
Commission on Labour has been set up as per resolution issued on   15.10.1999   
which   will   dispassionately  look  into   these   aspects 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
and suggest appropriate changes in the labour legislation/labour policy. In 
developing the framework for its recommendations, the Commission will, 
inter-alia, take into account the emerging economic environment i nvolving 
rapid technological changes, requiring response in terms of change in 
methods, timings and conditions of work in industry, trade and services, 
globalisation of economy, liberalisation of trade and industry and emphasis 
on international competitiveness, and the need for bringing the existing laws 
in tune with the future labour market needs and demands and the minimum 
level of labour protection and welfare measures and the basic institutional 
framework for ensuring the same, in a manner which is conducive to a 
flexible labour market and adjustments necessary for furthering technological 
change and economic growth. While bringing changes in the Labour Laws all 
concerned including Workers' organisatio ns and Employes organisations are 
consulted.

implementation of two schemes, for rehabilitation of children withdrawn 
from work, namely the Scheme of Na tional Child Labour Projects (NCLPs)

Causes of Poverty 
1430. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state: 
 whether it is a fact that in the year 2000, sixty per cent of the people of 
the country are still living Below the Poverty Line; 
 if so, what are the causes of such poverty; 
 the manner in which Government plan to bring people above poverty 
line, at least fifty per cent of the poverty stricken lot; and 
 whether it is a fact that poverty has increased in the country during the 
economic reforms from 1991 to 2001? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and (b) The Planning Commission estimates 
percentage of persons living below the poverty line at National and State level 
from the large sample surveys on cons umer expenditure conducted by the 
National Sample Survey (NSS) Organisation. The last such survey was 
conducted in the 55th Round of the NSS covering the period July 1999 to 
June 2000. On the basis of the 30-day recall tabulation in the Key Results of 
the 55th Round large sample survey of Hosuehold Consumer Expenditure in 
India carried out by the National Sample Survey Organisation, the percentage 
of persons living below the poverty line in the country in 1999-2000 is 
estimated as 26.1%. 
(c) There is a three-pronged action to alleviate and reduce the poverty in 
the country. These are: (i) acceleration of economic growth, (ii) human, and 
social development through literacy, education,   health,   nutrition,   meeting   
of   the   minimum   needs, 
elevation of social and economic status of  the weaker sections of the society, 
etc., and (iii) direct attack on poverty through employment and income 
generating programmes and assets-building for the poor. 
The increase in income of the people living below the poverty line occur 
from the joint impact of general growth process and direct income generation 
of the poor arising from various anti-poverty 
196 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
programmes introduced from time to time by the Government for their 
upliftment. Since the Sixth Five year Plan (1980—85), the Government has 
been implementing employment and asset generation schemes for the 
upliftment of the people living below the poverty line. These schemes are 
mainly of two types, self-employment and wage employment. Integrated 
Rural Development Programme (IRDP) has been the major self-employment 
programme and it has been in operation in all the blocks of the country since 
1980. The wage employment programme initially was National Rural 
Employment Programme (NREP) during the Sixth Plan period. In the 
Seventh Plan, another wage employment programme under the name Rural 
Labour Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP) was introduced. Then 
in 1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was launched by merging the 
National Rural Employment Programme and the Rural Labour Employment 
Guarantee Programme, and it became the main wage-employment programme. 
In addition, several programmes to help the poor were also in operation until 
March, 1999. These programmes are: Million Wells Scheme (MWS), 
Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS), Development of Women and Children 
in Rural Areas (DWCRA), Training of Rural Youth for Self-Employment 
(TRYSEM), Supply of Improved Toolkits to Rural Artisans (SITRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, these Programme, excepting EAS and JRY have 
been restructured into  single self-employment programme called the 
Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the primary objectives of 
focussed approach to poverty alleviation, capitalising advantages of group 
lending, and overcoming the problems associated with multiplicity of 
programmes. Also, from 1st April, 1999, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has 
been restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) with the 
primary objective of creation of demand driven community village 
infrastructure including durable assets at the village level and assets to enable 
the rural poor to increase the opportunities for sustained employment. Its 
secondary objective is generation of supplementary employment for the 
unemployed poor in the rural areas. The wage employment under the 
programme is given to Below Poverty Lines (BPL) families. 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
From 1.12.1997, Swama Jayanti Sahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is the main 
poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, which has 
subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation programmes, viz., Nehru 
Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Services for the Poor (UBSP), Prime 
Minister's Integrated Urban Poverty Eradication Programme (PMIUPEP), seeks to 
provide gainful employment to unemployed or underemployed urban and 
educated up to IX standard for setting up self-employment ventures or provision 
of wage employment. The implementation of SJSRY is relying on suitable 
community structures on the UBSP pattern and delivery of inputs under this 
programme is through the medium of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and such 
community structure. 
(d) The estimate of poverty calculated from the 50th Round large sample survey 
on consumer expenditure conducted by the National Sample Survey Organisation 
(NSSO) was 35.97% for the year 1993-94. The data from the latest large survey 
of the 55th Round on a 30 day basis indicate a poverty ratio of 26.1% for 1999-
2000. These figures are not strictly comparable due to methodological differences.

36% in 1993-94. The estimates of poverty in 1999-2000 are calculated as 
26.1% on the basis of a 30-day recall period and 23.3% on the basis of a 7-
day recall period. This is a result of increase in income of the people living 
below the poverty line due to the joint impact of general growth process and 
direct income generation of the poor arising from various anti-poverty 
programmes introduced from time to time by the Government for their 
upliftment. 
Rural population Below Poverty Line in Gujarat 
1432. SHRI ANANTRAY DEVSHANKER DAVE: Will the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 the percentage of rural population living Below Poverty Line at present 
in Gujarat; 
 the comparative figures of the other States as well as nation as a 
whole; and 
 the steps being taken or proposed to be reduce the percentage of 
poverty in the State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) The Planning Commission estimates 
percentage of persons living below the poverty line at national and state level 
from the large sample surveys on consumer expenditure conducted by the 
National Sample Survey (NSS) Organisation. The last such survey was 
conducted in the 55th Round of the NSS covering the period July 1999 to 
June 2000. On the basis of the 30-day recall tabulation in the Key Results of 
the 55th    Round    large    sample    survey    of   Household    Consumer 
199 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
Expenditure in India carried out by the National Sample Survey Organisation, the 
percentage of rural population living below the poverty line in Gujarat in 1999-
2000 is estimated as 13.17%. 
 The comparative estimates of poverty for other states and at national level 
are Annexed as statement (See below). 
 There is a three-pronged action to alleviate and reduce the poverty in the 
country. These prongs are: (i) accelera tion of economic growth, (ii) human 
and social development through literacy, education, health, nutrition, 
meeting of the minimum needs, elevatio n of social and economic status of 
the weaker sections of the society, et c., and (iii) direct attack on poverty 
through employment and income generating programmes and assets-building for 
the poor. 
The increase in income of the people living below the poverty line occurs from 
the joint impact of general growth process and direct income generation of the 
poor arising from various anti-poverty programmes introduced from time to time 
by the Government for their upliftment. Since the Sixth Five Year Plan (1980—
85), the Government has been implementing employment and asset generation 
schemes for the upliftment of the people living below the poverty line. These 
schemes are mainly of two types, self-employment and wage employment. 
Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) has been the major self-
employment programme and it has been in operation in all the blocks of the 
country since 1930. The wage employment programme initially was National Rural 
Employment Programme (NREP) during the Sixth Plan period. In the Seventh 
Plan, another wage employment programme (RLEGP) was introduced. Then in 
1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was launched by merging the National Rural 
Employment Programme and the Rural Labour Employment Guarantee 
Programme, and it became the main wage-employment programme. In addition, 
several programmes to help the poor were also in operation until March, 1999.   
These   programmes   are:   Million   Wells   Scheme   (MWS), 
200 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS), Development of Women and Children in 
Rural Areas (DWCRA), Training of Rural Youth for Self-Employment 
(TRYSEM), Supply of Improved Toolkits to Rural Artisans (SITRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, these programmes, excepting EAS and JRY have been 
restructured into single self-employment programme called the Swarnajayanti Gram 
Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the primary objectives of focussed approach to 
poverty alleviation, capitalising advantages of group lending, and overcoming the 
problems associated with multiplicity of programmes. Also, from 1st April, 1999, 
Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has b een restructured as Jawahar Gram 
Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) with the primary objective of creation of demand driven 
community village infrastructure including durable assests at the village level and 
assets to enable the rural poor to increase the opportunities for sustained 
employment. Its secondary objective is generation of s upplementary 
employment for the unemployed poor in the rural areas. The wage employment 
under the programme is given to Below Poverty Lines (BPL) families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swarna Jayanti Sahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is the main 
poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY which has 
subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation programmes, viz., Nehru 
Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Services for the Poor (UBSP), Prime 
Minister's Integrated Urban Poverty Eradication Programme (PMIUPEP), seeks to 
provide gainful employment to unemployed or underemployed urban and educated 
up to DC standard for setting up self employment ventures or provision of wage 
employment. The implementation of SJSRY is relying on suitable community 
structures on the UBSP pattern and delivery of inputs under this programme is 
through the medium of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and such community 
structure.

Unsolved Bask Problems 
1433. SHRI K.M. KHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 what are the reasons that despite our long and short-term planning, the 
basic problems like safe drinking water, elementary education, health, power and 
poverty are still unsolved; 
 whether Government are considering to take all these issues seriously; 
 if so, the details thereof; and 
 if not, the reasons tnerefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Considerable success has been achieved in 
increasing the coverage of our population with safe drinking water, elementary 
education, health and power and in reducing poverty through planned 
development. Yet, there is scope for achieving much greater success. 
The reasons for the shortfall in achie ving the objective of full coverage of 
drinking water supply are non-sustainability of water resources, unscientific drawal 
of ground water, deforestation and lack of protection, poor quality of construction 
and maintenance, non involvement of people in design, operation and 
maintenance and neglect of traditional water management strategies. As regards 
elementary education, the problem areas are high drop out rates, the lack of 
education of the girl child and of children belonging to weaker sections and those 
in inaccessible areas not served by elementary schools. 
In the area of Primary Health, consid erable success has been achieved in 
reducing Infant Mortality Rates (IMRs) and death rates accompanied by rise in 
life expectancy through control of communicable diseases, greater access of 
people in primary health facilities and widespread immunization. However, in the 
last decade, IMRs have tended to stagnate and new diseases, which are expensive 
to treat, have emerged. Access to Primary Health Care facilities are still limited 
in certain areas. As regards power in the rural areas, the 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
Rural Electrification Programme in the States is implemented by the State 
Electricity Boards (SEBs). The programme has slowed down during Eighth and 
Ninth Five Year Plan mainly because the SEBs poor financial condition. 
There has been a decline in the incidence of poverty from 54.88 per cent in 
1973-74 to 38.86 per cent in 1987-88 to 35.97 per cent in 1993-94 and to 26.10 
per cent in 1999-2000, which is impressive. 
(b) to (d) Government is committed to address these issues and make 
significant progress in all the above sectors. To achieve the target of safe 
drinking water, action would include; restrictions on withdrawal of ground water, 
people's control over management of water supply schemes and recharging of 
ground water through afforestation and watershed development. As regards the 
objective of Universal Elementary Education (UEE), a holistic and convergent 
approach to implement UEE in a mission mode will be undertaken with the 
central objective of mobilizing all the resources, human, financial and 
institutional necessary for achieving UEE. In the sector of Primary Health Care, 
every effort will be undertaken to streamline and improve efficiency and to bring 
accountability to the primary health care infrastructure in the country with the 
objective of bringing about significant reductions in IMRs and birth rates 
through improvements in reproductive health care, greater access to PHC 
facilities and provision of adequate referral services. 
Power sector in the rural areas is expected to improve through the improvement 
in the financial health of SEBs by launching of the Accelerated Power 
Development Programme. Assistance to States for village electrification is 
proposed to be extended on priority. 
In order to tackle the problem of poverty in the country, imphasis will be placed 
on agriculture through greater investments, both public and private. The focus 
would be on stimulating ground water development in the eastern region and 
watershed development in the plateau regions of Central India. Self employment 
would become a micro-finance programme through greater participation of banks 
and provision of necessary linkages to make selected activities viable. Marginal 
and small farmers, artisans, forest gatherers and unskilled 
206

workers would be specially supported. Emphasis will be laid on development of 
rural infrastructure including roads and irrigation. In order to improve delivery, 
democratic decentralization, greater accountability and transparency will be 
introduced with greater involvement of people in the implementation and 
monitoring of programmes so that they are more effective in reaching the target 
population.

Statement-II 
Poverty Estimates for 1999-2000 
The Planning Commission has been estimating the incidence of poverty at 
national and State level using the methodology contained in the report of the 
Expert Group on Estimation of Proportion and Number of Poor (Lakdawala 
Committee) and applying it to consumption expenditure data from the large 
sample surveys on consumer expe nditure, conducted periodically by the 
National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO). Poverty estimates for the year 
1973-74, 1977-78, 1983, 1987-88 and 1993-94 made on this basis were 
released by the Government of India, Press Information Bureau on 11th 
March, 1997. 
2. The NSSO has now released the key results of the latest large 
sample survey data on consumer expenditure (55th Round), covering 
the period of July, 1999 to June, 2000 (see Report No. 454 
(55/1.0/2). Two sets of different distributions of consumer 
expenditure from the 55th Round have been reported because of 
experimenting with the method of data collection. In the earlier large 
scale surveys, the NSSO estimated  monthly per capita consumption 
expenditure on the basis of responses using a 30-day recall period 
though data were collected for some of the non-food items using 
reference periods of both 30 days and 365 days from the same 
household. In the 55th Round, consumption expenditure on clothing, 
footwear, medical (institutional) and durable goods were collected by 
using a 365 days recall period. In the case of all other non-food 
items, the 30 days recall period was used as earlier. The data 
regarding consumption of food items were collected by using two 
different reference periods of last 30 days and last 7 days from the 
same household in that order. The two sets of data so collected were 
tabulated and the corresponding distributions of persons by monthly 
per capita consumption expenditure were included in the report, 
though the data based on 7 days reference period for the food items 
were collected only for investigating the suitability of the shorter 
reference period. 
3. Since   both   consumer  expenditure   distributions   have   been 
211 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
published, the Planning Commission has estimated poverty from both 
distributions reported by the NSSO, using the accepted methodology. State 
specific poverty lines have been estima ted using the original State specific 
poverty lines identified by the Lakdawala Committee and updating them to 
1999-2000 prices using the Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers 
(CHAL) for rural households and the Consumer Price Index of Industrial 
Workers (CPHW) for urban households. These poverty lines are given in 
Table 1 (See below). The poverty lines have th en been used in conjunction 
with each of the two consumption distribut ions, to estimate the percentage of 
people below the poverty line (poverty ratio) for each State. As in the past, 
separate estimates have been made for rural urban areas for each State, which 
are then combined into a State level estimate. 
4. The consumer expenditure data of the 55th Round on a 30 days 
recall basis yields a poverty ratio for 1999-2000 of 27.09% in rural 
areas, 23.62% in urban areas and 26 .10% for the country as a whole 
in 1999-2000 (Table 2) (see below). The corresponding figures from 
the 7 days recall period are 24.02% in rural areas, 21.59% in urban 
areas and 23.33% for the country as a whole (Table 3) (see below). 
 Although the 7 days estimates used in Table 3 are being reported in the 
interest of transparency, it should be noted that the NSS Governing Council 
has not yet decided to switch from the 30 days basis for food items to the 7 
days basis. For the present, the 30 days estimates reported in Table 2 are 
being used as the appropriate estimate of poverty. 
 The change in the methodology regarding the measurement of durable 
consumer goods from a 30 days recall period in earlier large sample surveys 
to a 365 days recall period in the 55th Round implies that the 30 days estimate 
for 1999-2000 in Table 2 may not be fully comparable with the earlier estimate. 
This fact needs to be kept in mind in assessing trends over time. However, 
improvement in methodology of collecting data is a continuing exercise.

1435. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: W ill the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that Government have given the responsibility to 
evaluate the KBK districts work to an N.G.O. which was very much opposed by

 the amount given for the development of KBK districts during the last two 
years; 
 whether State Government could spend the fund in time; and 
 whether the State Government has submitted a long term 
proposal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) Planning Commission had assigned a study on the KBK 
districts to an NGO. The study has since been withdrawn as the State Government 
was opposed to it and because the NGO could not complete the work in time. 
(b) In addition to the flow of funds from Central Plan and 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, Additional Central Assistance of 
Rs. 103.60 crore has been released to the State Government for the 
KBK districts in the last two years. 
 The State Government has reported an expenditure of Rs. 116.90 crore 
till 31st January, 2001. 
 The Revised Long Term Action Plan (1998-99 to 2006-07) for the KBK 
districts which has been prepared by the State Government consists of Central Plan 
and Centrally Sponsored Schemes in various sectors, namely agriculture, 
horticulture, watershed development, afforestation, irrigation, health, drinking water, 
emergency feeding, welfare of SCs/STs and rural connectivity. 
Special Category States 
1436. SHRI   RAMACHANDRA   KHUNTIA:  Will  the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) the criteria of declaring a State as a special category State and 
219 

RAJYA SABHA [8 March, 2001] 
what are the basic advantage of being declared as special-category State; 
 whether the Chief Minister of Orissa and alt major political parties have' 
been demanding to declare Orissa as special category State since many years; 
and 
 in the face of devastating dama ge caused by super cyclone, dr ought 
and flood, whether Government would declared the State as a special category 
State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) The main criteria for 
declaring a State as a Special category State are : 
(i) hilly and difficult terrain, (ii) low population density, (in) weak resource 
base and (iv) overall economic and infrastructure! backwardness. These 
States are strategically situated along international borders of the country, 
have sizeable tribal population and most of them have been formed from small 
Union Territories or districts of some other States. The principal advantage of 
being a special category State is that 90% of the Central Assistance is given 
as grant, whereas for Non-special category States only 30% is given as grant. 
 Yes, Sir. such requests have been made since 1991. 
 Devastation by cyclone or other natural calamities are not a criterion for 
eligibility to be a special category State.

Bringing wasteland under Agriculture 
1458. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that the ISRO Chief Shri K. Kasturirangan, while 
speaking at the Indian Science Congress held in Delhi, has said that 45 
million out of 64 million hectares of so called wasteland can be brought 
under some type of Agriculture; 
 if so, what are the details thereof; and 
 what other revelations were made by the ISRO Chief on the occasion? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) Shri K. Kasturirangan, 
Chairman, ISRO in his presentation on "Space Technology and Applicaitons 
for Food, Nutrition and Environment Security" at the 88th Indian Science 
Congress held in New Delhi, had mentioned that satellite images have been 
used to map wastelands in the country for the Ministry of Rural 
Development. A Technical Task Group, constituted by Planning Commission 
and Ministry of Rural Development, had arrived at the definition of the 
wastelands as those degraded and under-utilised lands that could be brought 
under vegetative cover with reasonable. effort, and also a 13 fold 
classification of the wast elands. He added that the Ministry of Rural 
Development bad recently published a Wasteland Atlas of India, based on the 
satellite mapping, wherein it has been stated that a total of about 4 million 
hectares, of the country is under watelands. He observed that, out of these 64 
million hectares, about 45 million 
236 

[8 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
hectares could be made culturable- meaning that the productive use of land 
could be enhanced by appropriate r eclamation measures for agriculture, 
forestry, agro-horticlutre, horticulture, grasslands, silivipasture, etc. 
(c) In the presentation, Chairman, ISRO outlined how space technology 
inputs, both from remote sensing and satellite communicaitons, could benefit 
programmes of enhancing security of food, nutrition and environment in the 
country. He gave examples of the usage of the satellite images for national-
level inventorymapping of various natural resource themes for CentraMState 
Government agencies. He specifica lly illustrated the Ministry of 
Agriculture's project for Crop Acreage and Production Estimation, Ministry 
of Rural Development's project for identification of target areas for 
groundwater exploration and recharge, Ministry of Water Resource's 
programme for suface water inventory and command area management, 
Ministry of Agriculture's project for monitoring of salt* effected and water 
logged areas, Ministry of Rural Development's programme for integrated 
approach to land and water resources management in watersheds, flood 
inundation and agricultural drought monitoring and the pilot programme for 
establishing a National Natural Resources Information System. Lastly, he 
envisioned the need for a national endeavor on Precision Farming by adopting 
high technology inputs.

SHRI B.J. PANDA (Orissa): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I rise to 
support the Motion of Thanks on the President's Address moved by 
Shri T.N. Chaturvedi. At the outset, in his" Address to the Joint Session 
of Parliament, the President first referred to the great tragedy that 
befell Gujarat on this Republic Day. Sir, being from the State of Orissa, 
I can appreciate the enormous diffi culty the State has gone through, 
the enormous tragedy that it had to face. The people of Gujarat have 
shown exemplary courage and fortitude in coming out of this great 
disaster. In particular, one must thank the tireless efforts put in not only 
by millions of people of Gujarat but also thousands of other citizens 
who visited the State to lend their support and also many non-
Governmental organisations that worked tirelessly to rescue people 
and rebuild Gujarat. However, it is my painful duty at this point of time 
to draw a contrast between this and the treatment received from the 
Central Government by Orissa when it was hit by the most devastating 
cyclone ever recorded in our hist ory just 15 months ago. Sir, 14 
districts in the State of Orissa we re completely devastated, The State 
Government has been working round the clock and has built far in 
excess of 50,000 houses to rehabilitat e the people, By the end of this 
month one lakh houses will be construc ted. But that is nowhere near 
adequate. There is stark contrast in  the kind of funds that have been 
allocated for the rehabilitation work in Gujarat vis-a-vis the kind of 
funds that have been allocated for Orissa. It is ironic that a State that is 
more developed, a State that has far better insurance cover gets 
greater attention

than the poorest State in the country by the latest reckoning. Orissa is 
still reeling. Its economy is comp letely devastated after what has 
happened at the end of 1999. The State requires tremendous, 
continuous support to get back on t he rail. Media reports have pointed 
out that many victims in Gujara t are showing courage and even 
refusing the aid that is being granted to them. The State of Orissa has 
no such luxury because thousands of affected people are still at the 
bottom and below the poverty line. They have no such luxury and they 
need the help of the country. A National Disaster Management

The President has also talked about the Eleventh Finance 
Commission's report. I sha'l be failing in my duty if I do not speak out 
on the injustice done by the Eleventh Finance Commission to my 
State, Orissa, I have just talked about the super-cyclone which befell it. 
Sir, the State has gone through some kinds of flood, droughts and 
cyclones year after year in the recent past and it is in a serious 
financial crunch which can be seen from the fact that more than 50 per 
cent of the State's budget goes only fo r making interest payments. It is 
known internationally and it is well understood that when any country 
or any State pays 20 or 25 per cent of  its budget as interest charges, it 
is in a serious fiscal crunch. My State has gone beyond 50 per cent 
and this is the situation that has  been inherited from decades of bad 
governance. Sir, the State of Orissa deserves to be categorised as a 
'special category State', which would provide the necessary financial 
structure, for it to be put back on the rails. This is  particularly important

poorest State, has taken some of the early and bold steps towards 
economic reform, which the Presi dent's Address has given so much 
emphasis on. It is the State which has had the first reform in the power

country and yet the State itself is in a fiscal mess. There are many 
other bold steps that the State is taking. For example, recently, its
